translations.text: Dearest people, a few days ago we read this gospel aloud before you, which belongs to the service of this day, in order to explain the gospel narrative in its sequence;
but we did not touch on the exposition any further than belonged to the honour of that day. Now we will run over the same gospel narrative again and give an exposition concerning this present feast.

Matthew the Evangelist said, "Cum natus esset Iesus in Bethleem Iudæ, in diebus Herodis regis, ecce Magi ab oriente uenerunt Hierosolimam, dicentes, Ubi est qui natus est Rex Iudeorum?" [When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying, Where is he who is born King of the Jews?]
and the rest. "When the Saviour was born in the Judean Bethlehem, in the days of King Herod,
behold, three astrologers came from the eastern part of the world to the city of Jerusalem, asking thus, Where is the King of the Jewish people, who has been born?" etc.

This day is called Epiphania Domini, that is, the day of God's manifestation. On this day Christ was made manifest to the three kings, who sought him from the eastern part of the world with threefold gifts.
Again, after the passing of years, he was made manifest to the world at his baptism on this day, when the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, [?]
rested upon him, and the Father's voice sounded loudly from heaven, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him."
Also on this day he turned water into noble wine, and by that he showed that he is the true Creator, who could change created things.
Because of these three things this feast-day is called God's manifestation. On the very day of his birth he was shown to three shepherds in the land of the Jews, through the angel's message.
On that same day he was made known to the three astrologers in the east, through the bright star; but it was on this day that they came with their gifts.

It was fitting that a rational angel should make him known to the rational Jews, who knew God's law, and that to the heathens, who did not know divine reason, he should be revealed not through a voice but through a sign.
The Jewish shepherds signified the spiritual shepherds, that is, the apostles, whom Christ chose from the Jewish people to be shepherds and teachers for us.
The astrologers, who were living in heathendom, signified all the heathen peoples, who were turned to God through the teaching of the apostles, who were of the Jewish nation.

Truly the psalmist wrote about Christ that he is the cornerstone that joins the two walls together, because he joined his chosen ones from the Jewish people and the faithful from the heathens, like two walls, into one church;
Concerning this Paul the apostle said, "The Saviour at his coming preached peace to us who were far off, and peace to those who were near."
He is our peace, who made both into one, casting down the former enmities in himself."
The Jews who believed in Christ were nearer to him in place, and also through their knowledge of the old law;
we were very far off, both in place and through ignorance; but he gathered us with one faith to the high cornerstone, that is, into the unity of his church.
The eastern astrologers saw a new, bright star, not in the heavens among the other stars, but it travelled alone between heaven and earth.
Then they understood that the strange star signified the birth of the true King in the land over which it glided;

and therefore they came to the kingdom of Judea, and greatly frightened the wicked king Herod with their tidings; for without doubt earthly wickedness was put to shame when the heavenly majesty was revealed.
It is clear that the astrologers acknowledged Christ as true man, when they asked, "Where is he who is born?"
They recognized him as true King, when they said, "King of the Jews." They worshipped him as true God, when they said, "We have come so that we may pray to him."
God could easily have guided them by the star to the city in which the child was, just as he revealed his birth by the rising of the star;
but he wanted the Jewish scribes to read the prophecy about him, and so make known the place of his birth, so that they would be saved
if they were willing to worship Christ together with the astrologers; but if they were not willing, then they would be condemned by that very revelation.
The astrologers went and worshipped, and the Jewish scribes, who had pointed out the place of birth through learning from books, stayed behind.
All creatures recognized the coming of their Creator, except the impious Jews alone.
The heavens recognized their Creator when they showed a new star at his birth. The sea recognized him when Christ walked mightily over its waves with dry soles.
The sun recognized him when, at his passion, it hid its light from midday until the ninth hour. The stones recognized him when they burst into pieces at his death.
The earth recognized him when it all trembled at his resurrection. Hell recognized him when it let its captives go against its will.
And yet the hard-hearted Jews would not, for all these signs, acknowledge the true Creator, whom the dumb creatures understood and made manifest by signs.
Yet they were not all unbelieving without exception; from their race came both prophets and apostles, and many thousands of believing people.
When the astrologers turned to the king, the star became invisible to them;
and afterwards, when they turned to the child, they saw the star again, and it then led them to the house in which he dwelt.
It did not glide before them the whole way, but after they came to the land of the Jews, it was then their guide, until it stood still above Christ's lodging.
Herod signified the devil; and whoever turns from God to the devil loses God's grace, that is, the enlightenment of his mind, just as the astrologers lost the star when they turned to the cruel king.
But if he afterwards resolutely forsakes the devil, then he finds again the grace of the Holy Spirit, which enlightens his heart and leads him to Christ.
We should also know that there were certain heretics who said that every person is born according to the positions of the stars, and that his fate befalls him through their courses,
and they took as support for their error the fact that a new star arose when the Lord was born in the flesh, and they said that the star was his fate.
Let this error depart from believing hearts, that there is any fate other than the Almighty Creator, who provides life for every person according to his merits.
Man is not created for the sake of the stars; rather, the stars are created to give light to people at night.
When the star glided along and led the astrologers, and pointed out to them the child's dwelling, it showed that it was Christ's creature and rightly served its Creator; but it was not his fate.
Again we ask that no believing person defile his faith with this error.

Indeed, Rebecca, Isaac's wife, bore twins, Jacob and Esau, at one time, so that Jacob held his elder brother Esau by the foot at the birth, and yet they were not alike in character or in the merits of their lives.
Truly, holy scripture says that God loved Jacob and hated Esau; not because of fate, but because of their different deserts.

It happens very often that the queen and the female slave give birth at the same hour, and yet the prince rises by his birth to the high royal throne, and the slave woman's son remains in servitude all his life.

Now foolish people often say that they must live according to fate, as if God compelled them to evil deeds! But we will extinguish the idle lies of these foolish people with the depth of the divine scriptures.
The Almighty Creator created angels through his divine power, and because of his great righteousness gave them their own free choice,
so that they could continue in eternal bliss through obedience, and could also lose that bliss, not because of fate, but because of disobedience.
His deep righteousness would not force them to either, but gave them their own choice; for it is righteousness that each person be allowed his own choice.
For his righteousness would have been made void if he had bent them to his service by compulsion, or if he had pushed them into wickedness.
Then some of the angels misused their own free will, and through pride turned themselves into accursed devils.
Again, when the Creator who rules as Trinity made mankind, he gave Adam and Eve their own free will, so that either, through obedience,
they might live in bliss for ever and ever, without death, with all their offspring, or, through disobedience, they would become mortal.
But when they broke God's command and obeyed the teaching of the accursed devil, they became mortal, and through their own choice they made themselves guilty, both themselves and all their offspring;
and even if mercy had never afterwards been shown to mankind, any more than it is to the devils, God's justice would still have been entirely blameless.
But afterwards the great mercy of our Lord redeemed us through his incarnation, if we obey his commandments with all our heart.
Truly, those who now forsake God through their own choice and the devil's instigation, God also forsakes to eternal perdition.
The Almighty Creator knew well, before he created his creatures, what was to come.
He knew for certain the number both of the chosen angels and of the chosen people, and also of the proud spirits and of the wicked people who perish through their wickedness;
but he predestined no one to evil, because he himself is all goodness; nor did he destine anyone to destruction, because he is true life.
He predestined the chosen to eternal life, because he knew that they would become such through his grace and their own obedience.
He would not predestine the wicked to his kingdom, because he knew that they would become such through their own transgression and perversity.
Hold this firmly in your hearts: that the Almighty and Righteous God compels no one to sin, but he knows beforehand nonetheless which people will sin of their own will.
Why then should he not justly punish the evil that he abhors? He loves all good and righteousness, because he is by nature good and righteous;
and he hates all those who work unrighteousness, and destroys those who speak lies. Truly, those who believe in God are guided by the Holy Spirit.
Our turning to God does not come from ourselves but from God's grace, just as the apostle says, "By God's grace you are kept in the faith."
Those who do not believe refuse through their own choice, not through fate, because fate is nothing but a false notion;

and truly nothing happens by fate, but all things are ordered by God's judgement, who said through his prophet, "I search the hearts and the loins of men, and give to each according to his ways and according to his own devising."

Let no one ascribe his evil deeds to God, but let him ascribe them first to the devil, who deceived mankind, and to Adam's transgression; but most of all to himself, because evil pleases him and good does not please him.
Yet offspring are often made guilty through the wicked deeds of their forefathers, if they imitate them in evil.
But if the offspring is righteous, then he lives in his righteousness and by no means bears the sins of his ancestors.
Let no one be so impious as to curse Adam or Eve, who now reign with God in heaven, but let him rather earn God's mercy by turning his own will to obedience to his Creator and to his commandments;
because no one is saved except through the grace of the Saviour Christ: that grace he prepared and predestined in his eternal counsel before the foundation of the world.
My brothers, you have now heard about the false notion that idle people call fate: let us now take up the exposition of the gospel where we left it before.
The astrologers went into the child's lodging and found him with his mother.
Then they stretched themselves out on the ground and worshipped Christ, and opened their treasure-chests and offered him a threefold gift: gold, incense and myrrh.
Gold is fitting for a king; incense belongs to the service of God; with myrrh people wrap the bodies of the dead, so that they are slow to rot.
These three astrologers worshipped Christ and offered him symbolic gifts. The gold signified that he is the true King.
The incense signified that he is true God. The myrrh signified that he was then mortal; but he now continues immortal for eternity.
There were some heretics who believed that he was God, but they did not believe at all that he reigned everywhere. They offered Christ spiritual incense, and would not offer him gold.
Then there were other heretics who believed that he was the true King, but they denied that he was God. These, without doubt, offered him gold and would not offer incense.

Some heretics confessed that he was true God and true King, and denied that he took on mortal flesh. These indeed brought him gold and incense, and would not bring the myrrh of the mortality he had taken on.
My brothers, let us offer gold to our Lord, by confessing that he is the true King and reigns everywhere.
Let us offer him incense, in that we believe that he who at that time appeared as man was ever God.
Let us bring him myrrh, by believing that he, who cannot suffer in his divinity, was mortal in our flesh.
He was mortal in his human nature before his passion, but from now on he is immortal, just as we all shall be after the general resurrection.
We have said how these threefold gifts relate to Christ. We will also say how they relate to us, according to the moral sense.
By gold, indeed, wisdom is signified, as Solomon said: "A desirable treasure of gold lies in the mouth of the wise."
By incense holy prayer is shown, of which the psalmist sang: "Lord, let my prayer be sent up like burning incense in your sight."
Through myrrh the mortality of our flesh is represented; of which the holy Church says: "My hands dripped with myrrh."
We bring gold to the newborn King if we shine in his sight with the brightness of heavenly wisdom.
We bring him incense if, through earnestness in holy prayers, we set our thoughts alight on the altar of our heart, so that through heavenly longing we may give off a somewhat pleasant fragrance.
We offer him myrrh if we kill the desires of the flesh through abstinence. Myrrh, as we said before, causes dead flesh not to rot easily.
Truly, the dead flesh rots sinfully when the mortal body serves flowing lust, as the prophet said about certain people, "The beasts rotted in their dung."
The beasts rot in their dung when fleshly men end their days in the stench of their lust.
But if we offer the myrrh to God spiritually, then our mortal body will be kept from the stenches of lust through abstinence.
The astrologers signified something of great importance to us in returning to their own country by another way.
Our country, truly, is paradise, and we cannot return to it by the way we came.
The first-created man and all his offspring were driven out of the joy of paradise through disobedience, and for eating the forbidden food,
and through pride, when he wished to be better than the Almighty Creator had made him.
But we have great need to avoid the deceitful devil by another way, so that we may happily come to our homeland, for which we were created.
Through obedience, abstinence and humility we must walk with one mind to our homeland, and by holy virtues regain the country that we lost through sins.
Rightly was the deceitful Herod deceived by the astrologers, and he did not come to Christ, because he sought him with a treacherous mind.
He signified the false hypocrites, who seek God with pretence, and never find him.
He is to be sought with a truthful heart and a steadfast mind, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
